title: Proof pages for a two-sided marketplace
excerpt: A proof page for the scarce side shows the constraint, the decision, and one real match. Screenshots without a decision are decoration. End on how to join.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen, the kind of concrete record a marketplace proof page should feel like.
caption: A person signing a paper document with a pen. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a marketplace case study open with?
faqs.answer: Open with the constraint that made the match hard, in the units the scarce side already uses. Name the decision someone made, including what you gave up. Put both in the first screen, because most visitors will not read the whole page. A gallery of screenshots does not substitute for that opening.

faqs.question: Can we publish a case study without customer quotes?
faqs.answer: Yes. Describe the match, the constraint, and the outcome in plain sentences. Use a quotation only when the person said it and agreed to be cited. A sentence you wrote and put in their mouth is a larger risk than a page with no quotation marks at all.

faqs.question: How should a marketplace proof page end?
faqs.answer: End by telling a similar person on the side you need first how to join, what to have ready, and who the story is not for. Use the same join label as the rest of the site. A closing line about the future of the industry does not give them a door.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A two-sided marketplace case study page should show a constraint, a decision, and one concrete match. Screenshots with no decision are decoration. End on how a similar person on the side you need first can join.

Write the page for that side, not for an investor skimming a deck. The investor can read a metric in a meeting. The host, the carrier, or the worker is deciding whether your market behaves like the story.

## Start from the constraint

The constraint is what made the match hard. A city with almost no diners. A lane nobody wanted on a Friday. A credential that took three weeks to check. A payout rule that nearly lost the first host. If the story has no constraint, it is an advertisement, and the scarce side can tell.

Name the constraint in the first paragraph, in their units. "We had four approved kitchens and no public demand in one neighborhood." "The carrier would not accept the load unless the rate was visible before dispatch." Leave the company's internal codename out. Leave the adjective "exciting" out. The constraint is interesting because it is specific.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on reading is the editing rule. People have time for about a quarter of the text on a page they actually open. The constraint and the decision have to live in that quarter, which on a proof page means the opening and the headings, not a caption under the third screenshot. A beautiful scroll that reveals the point at the bottom is a scroll most people will not finish.

Put one match in the frame. A page that claims "dozens of success stories" and then shows a collage has refused to choose. Choose the match that most resembles the side you are still trying to recruit.

## Name the decision

A decision is a choice you could have made the other way. You capped the guest count. You showed the take rate before acceptance. You refused a category that would have grown the numbers and ruined the trust. You staffed the first month by hand instead of opening the city to anyone with an email address.

Write the decision as a sentence with a subject. "The founder confirmed every menu for six weeks." "We declined same-day bookings until hosts asked for them." Passive lines ("it was decided to prioritize trust") hide the person the about page just promised. If you cannot say who decided, you are not ready to publish the story.

Say what you gave up. A proof page that only records the upside reads as edited, because it is. The scarce side is looking for the tradeoff that will apply to them. If hosts gave up walk-in control in exchange for prepaid seats, say that. Someone who wants walk-ins can leave. Someone who wants prepaid seats can join. Both are better than a fog of "it went great."

Do not invent a quote to make the decision feel human. If a participant will say a sentence in their own words and stand by it, use that sentence and their name, with permission. If they will not, paraphrase the outcome without quotation marks. A fake quote is a worse risk than a plain paragraph.

## Show the match, not the chrome

The match is the object of the page. Who was on each side, what moved, what completed, and what each side received. A dinner for six at a stated price. A load picked up on a stated day. A shift that paid on the stated Friday.

Screenshots can support that, after the words. A screen is useful when it shows the moment of the decision: the rate before accept, the guest count the host locked, the checklist a family saw. A screen of an empty dashboard, a settings panel, or a marketing hero inside the product is furniture. Crop to the proof. If the interface is still ugly at that spot, a sentence may be more honest than a picture of a half-built tool.

Label examples. If the story is a composite, say composite, and do not attach a real person's neighborhood to a made-up night. If the story is real, you do not need to publish a last name, a street, or a face. You do need enough detail that a peer believes it happened.

One annotated image beats a gallery of twelve. The annotation should repeat the decision in a line: "Host locked eight seats. The ninth request was declined." That line is the case. The pixels are the evidence.

## Keep the numbers you can defend

A count belongs on the page when you can point at the records. Twelve completed dinners. One city. A payout time you actually hit. Percentages need a denominator. "90% satisfaction" with no count and no question text is a costume.

Skip comparative claims you cannot show. "Faster than the industry" requires an industry figure you are willing to cite and a measurement you ran the same way. If you do not have that, write "hosts were paid the Friday after the dinner" and stop. A peer can judge that sentence. They cannot judge a superlative.

Google's people-first guidance favors pages that demonstrate first-hand experience. A case study is first-hand only if someone on your side lived the constraint. Write it from that seat. A post assembled from analytics screenshots by someone who never spoke to the host will sound like it, and the next host will feel the distance.

If legal or privacy limits the detail, shrink the story rather than inflate the adjectives. "A licensed clinician in one state, twenty visits, payout on the published schedule" can be enough. Empty praise cannot replace the visits you are not allowed to describe.

## End on a similar person joining

The last block is an invitation with conditions. Who this story is for. Who it is not for. What they should have ready. The same join label you use everywhere else.

"If you host in this city and you can cook for a full table, apply as a host. Have a sample menu ready. If you need the platform to supply food or staff, this is the wrong market." That ending respects the reader who is a poor fit. It also tells the right reader that the door is the same door they saw on the homepage.

Do not end on "the future of connection." The future is not a next step. The next step is the application, the listing, or the credential upload. Repeat the response time you publish elsewhere, and keep it.

Link to the services block this story illustrates, if that page exists. A proof page that cannot point at a current offer is an archive piece. Archive pieces can be good. They should not be the only door on the site.

## What not to borrow from a product launch

Startup case-study templates want a hero metric, a pull quote, a logo, and a "challenge / solution / result" ladder that ends in software. Your reader is not buying software. They are lending you their kitchen, their truck, or their evening.

Use the ladder only if you translate it. The challenge is their constraint, not your lack of brand awareness. The solution is the decision, not "we built a platform." The result is the completed match, not a percentage lift in signups. Signup lift is your metric. Their metric is a night that paid, a lane that cleared, a shift that was staffed.

Keep the page short enough to reread. A thousand words of scene-setting before the decision will be skimmed down to the pictures, and we already know the pictures are not the point. Four or five short sections are plenty. If you have three strong matches, publish three pages. Do not stack them into one page that tries to prove the entire company.

## Review the page before you add design

Read the draft with the screenshots removed. If the constraint, the decision, and the match are still clear, the pictures are allowed to come back as evidence. If the draft collapses without the pictures, the pictures were doing a job the sentences skipped, and the sentences have to be rewritten first.

Check three consistencies against the live site. The fee in the story matches the pricing page. The refusal matches a services block. The join label matches the header. A proof page that remembers an old take rate is not nostalgia. It is a contradiction a careful applicant will screenshot.

Ask one person who resembles the subject, and who was not in the project, what they think they are being asked to do at the end. If they say "be impressed," the ending is still a trophy. If they can say who should apply and what to have ready, the page is done enough to design.

A proof page only works if the person can find it from the job they came to do. The next piece is [navigation for a two-sided marketplace](/blog/navigation-for-a-two-sided-marketplace), because the labels are the map to this story.

The public record of how a finished site can show its work, without a fog of metrics, sits in [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
